items.readable_text:
Content:
Decimals are a way of expressing fractions in an equivalent form that's often easier to work with.

Content:
For example, let's consider the fraction "one-tenth":

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{10}]

Content:
To express this fraction as a decimal, we write a zero [MATH: ({\color{red}0})] followed by a dot [MATH: (\,.)] (called the decimal point) followed by the fraction's numerator:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}1}{10} = {\color{red}{0}}{\color{blue}{.1}}]

Content:
Any fraction with a denominator of [MATH: 10] can similarly be written as a decimal.

Content:
For example, we can express six-tenths as a decimal as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}6}{10} = 0.{\color{blue}{6}}]

Content:
Note: Fractions with a denominator of [MATH: 10] are examples of decimal fractions. We'll meet more decimal fractions in this lesson.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Fractions with a denominator of [MATH: 100] can also be written as decimals. For this reason, they are also called decimal fractions.

Content:
When writing a fraction with a denominator of [MATH: 100,] we must remember the following crucial fact:

Content:
> Every fraction with a denominator of [MATH: 100] will have precisely two digits after the decimal point.

Content:
Let's see some examples:

Content:
- We express the fraction seventy-eight hundredths as a decimal as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}78}{100} = 0.{\color{blue}78}]
Notice that this decimal has two digits after the decimal point.
- We express the fraction three-hundredths as a decimal as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}3}{100} = 0.0{\color{blue}3}]
Notice that this decimal also has two digits after the decimal point.

Content:
Watch Out! When the numerator is smaller than [MATH: 10,] we must write an extra zero after the decimal point and before the numerator's digit. The following answers are not equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac{3}{100}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 0.3, \qquad 0.30, \qquad 00.3]

Content:
Finally, the fraction [MATH: \dfrac{1}{100}] is known as one-hundredth, and can also be written as a decimal:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}1}{100} = 0.0{\color{blue}{1}}]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Decimals are a way of expressing fractions in an equivalent form that's often easier to work with.

Content:
For example, let's consider the fraction "one-tenth":

Content:
To express this fraction as a decimal, we write a zero [MATH: ({\color{red}0})] followed by a dot [MATH: (\,.)] (called the decimal point) followed by the fraction's numerator:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}1}{10} = {\color{red}{0}}{\color{blue}{.1}}]

Content:
Any fraction with a denominator of [MATH: 10] can similarly be written as a decimal.

Content:
For example, we can express six-tenths as a decimal as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}6}{10} = 0.{\color{blue}{6}}]

Content:
Note: Fractions with a denominator of [MATH: 10] are examples of decimal fractions. We'll meet more decimal fractions in this lesson.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Fractions With Denominators of 100 as Decimals

Content:
Fractions with a denominator of [MATH: 100] can also be written as decimals. For this reason, they are also called decimal fractions.

Content:
When writing a fraction with a denominator of [MATH: 100,] we must remember the following crucial fact:

Content:

Content:
Let's see some examples:

- We express the fraction seventy-eight hundredths as a decimal as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}78}{100} = 0.{\color{blue}78}]
Notice that this decimal has two digits after the decimal point.
- We express the fraction three-hundredths as a decimal as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}3}{100} = 0.0{\color{blue}3}]
Notice that this decimal also has two digits after the decimal point.

Content:
Watch Out! When the numerator is smaller than [MATH: 10,] we must write an extra zero after the decimal point and before the numerator's digit. The following answers are not equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac{3}{100}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 0.3, \qquad 0.30, \qquad 00.3]

Content:
Finally, the fraction [MATH: \dfrac{1}{100}] is known as one-hundredth, and can also be written as a decimal:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}1}{100} = 0.0{\color{blue}{1}}]
